title: Kindness & Gratitude Ritual
strapline: A small daily ritual of noticing kindness and naming what we're glad about — growing warm hearts and grateful eyes.
intent: Children learn to notice and name kindness — their own and others' — so caring becomes a visible, valued habit.
Children practise gratitude, tuning into the good and the people they're glad about, which lifts wellbeing.
Children build empathy and prosocial behaviour by celebrating helping, sharing and comforting out loud.
Children develop the language of appreciation and care — thank you, I liked it when, I'm glad.
Children experience a warm, connected community where being kind is who we are, not just a rule.
implementation: Weave a short ritual into a calm point of the day — a 'kindness caught' moment at group time, or a 'something I'm glad about' round at snack.
Notice real kindness specifically and warmly — 'you fetched a tissue for your friend, that was so kind' — rather than praising vaguely.
Keep gratitude concrete and small for little ones: a person, a food, a game, the sunshine — not abstract lists.
Model your own kindness and gratitude genuinely — 'I'm grateful you helped me tidy' — so it's lived, not lectured.
Make it visible: a kindness tree that grows a leaf for each kind act, or a gratitude jar filled through the week.
Keep it light and joyful, never a compulsory performance — an invitation to notice good, not a test.
key_questions: Did you see an act of kindness today?
What's something you're glad about right now?
How do you think it felt to be helped like that?
Who has been kind to you today?
What kind thing could you do for a friend?

impact.text: Children notice how others feel and act on it — kindness becomes a habit, not a rule.
Children copy and show kindness — pats, hugs, fetching things, comforting a friend.
Children take turns, share and contribute to a warm, fair group.
Children talk about feelings — their own and others' — and what helps.
Children take visible pride in kind acts and effort — 'I did it!'

enhancements: A kindness tree on the wall that grows a paper leaf or blossom for every kind act noticed.
A gratitude jar filled with children's 'glad about' notes, read back at the end of the week.
Kindness missions — small acts children choose to do for the room or each other.
A 'thank you' post-box for children to send appreciation to friends and staff.
Stories about kindness and helping rotated through the book corner to spark talk.

playing_exploring: Children explore what kindness looks and feels like through real acts and shared stories.
Building the kindness tree or gratitude jar makes the ritual hands-on and joyful.
active_learning: Being noticed for kindness motivates children to be kind again — a virtuous circle.
Children take initiative in kind acts, driven by the warm response they bring.
creating_thinking: Children take others' perspectives, imagining how a kind act feels to receive.
They begin to plan their own kindnesses and reflect on what they're grateful for.
